title: Black Sea Strikes Threaten Global Grain Supply as Exports Drop 60%
summary:
The Black Sea has become the most dangerous it has been since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine began on Feb. 24, 2022. Since mid-July, more than 210 strikes have hit commercial vessels, according to Ambrey, a British maritime risk firm. It attributes 125 strikes to Ukraine and 88 to Russia.

On the water, Ukrainian navy crews feel the danger firsthand. Cmdr. Mykola Lupar, 29, leads a patrol boat out of the port of Chornomorsk, and he says his crew can usually count their time on open water in minutes before rushing back to shore. "We are trying to find some windows in time between Russian attacks to patrol, to search for mines and some explosive materials," Lupar said. "It's very dangerous. For the merchant fleet, I would say there's almost no chance to stay safe in our waters."

The fighting is choking global grain. Russia and Ukraine together account for roughly a quarter of the world's wheat exports, and analysts estimate their combined exports are down 60% from last year. That has already pushed global wheat prices higher, and analysts warn they could spike further.

"It's not only a Ukrainian problem. This is a problem for the whole region," said Dmytro Barinov, president of the Ukrainian Ports Association. He warned that food shortages could soon be felt across the region, predicting that by October or November at the latest, "everybody will feel the shortage of food."

Each side blames the other. Russia's Defence Ministry insists it targets only military assets and accused a cargo ship struck Thursday in Chornomorsk of supplying the military. Barinov says Russia is hitting civilian ships, pointing to a July missile strike on the Golden Leo near Odesa that killed 10 people. Ukraine said the ship was carrying corn. Barinov compared the attacks to hunting, since merchant ships are slow, can't manoeuvre quickly and have no military defences: "It's like hunting for an elephant from a helicopter."

Ukraine has also struck Russian ships and ports. In August, a large missile and drone attack on Novorossiysk hit a naval base and damaged two major grain export terminals.

Insurance companies now treat a larger part of the Black Sea as high risk. More than 50 pieces of unexploded ordnance have been found outside Russian and Ukrainian waters this year, Ambrey says. Turkey-led efforts to secure a limited truce have so far failed, and a 2022 UN-Turkey grain deal collapsed after Russia refused to renew it.
why_it_matters: Because two countries at war supply so much of the world's wheat, this shows how a regional conflict can push up food prices and cause shortages thousands of miles away — global systems like food trade are tightly linked and easily broken.

background_read: The Black Sea is a large sea bordered by Ukraine, Russia, Turkey, Georgia, Romania and Bulgaria, and it is the main route for Ukrainian and Russian grain to reach world markets by ship. Ukraine and Russia are often called the 'breadbasket of Europe' because their rich soil produces enormous wheat, corn and sunflower crops. Chornomorsk, the port where Cmdr. Lupar's patrol boat sails from, is one of Ukraine's biggest Black Sea ports, near Odesa.

In July 2022, the United Nations (the world body where nearly every country is represented) and Turkey brokered the Black Sea Grain Initiative, which let ships carry grain out of Ukrainian ports under inspection. Russia withdrew from that deal and it collapsed, so Ukraine has since tried to keep exporting through its own corridor. Turkey controls the narrow straits linking the Black Sea to the Mediterranean, which is why it often acts as a mediator. Ambrey is a British maritime risk company that advises shipping firms about danger at sea.

perspectives.description: They argue Ukraine has the right to strike Russian ports and ships that help fund the war, pointing to the August attack on Novorossiysk, and that patrols and mine-clearing keep at least some shipping moving.
It insists its strikes target only military assets and accused the cargo ship hit Thursday in Chornomorsk of supplying the military, effectively denying that civilian shipping is the target.
They focus less on blame and more on the mechanism: more strikes make insurers mark the sea high risk, which raises costs, keeps ships away and pushes grain prices up regardless of who fires.
